title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons
statement: Each balloon spans [xstart, xend] on the x-axis. An arrow shot straight up at x bursts every balloon with xstart <= x <= xend. Return the minimum number of arrows needed to burst all balloons.

large_tests.gen_code:
import random
def gen():
    r = random.Random(48)
    return [[(lambda a: [a, a + r.randint(0, 100)])(r.randint(0, 10**6)) for _ in range(100000)]]

hints.1_question: One arrow can burst a whole group if they all share a common x. When is it safe to say 'this arrow is as far right as it can usefully be'?
hints.2_nudge: Sort by end. Shoot at the end of the first balloon; every balloon starting at or before that x is burst. A balloon starting after it needs a new arrow.
hints.3_big_hint: arrows = 0, end = -inf; for s, e in sorted by e: if s > end: arrows += 1; end = e.

known_bugs.name: touching balloons need separate arrows (>=)
known_bugs.followup: A balloon ending at 2 and one starting at 2 can both be hit at x = 2. Does your comparison allow that?

known_bugs.name: merges chains of overlaps (needs a common point, not just a chain)
known_bugs.followup: Balloons [1,3] and [4,7] each overlap [2,5], but is there one x that hits all three?

known_bugs.name: sorts by end but never starts a new group's end
known_bugs.followup: After you decide to shoot a new arrow, what should the 'current arrow position' become?

followups: How is this related to problem 435?
Why is shooting at the earliest end optimal?
